variants.title: Score the whole trajectory
variants.context: An agent run is scored end to end: declare the task contract, execute in a controlled world, score the decisions and recovery along the way, verify authoritative external state, then repeat under variation. The agent's own completion sentence is never the evidence.
variants.prompt: A team currently scores its agent by reading the final assistant message. Put the evaluation steps in order.

items.text: Read the external system to classify the effect as complete, partial, duplicate, or missing.
Run the agent against controlled tools while preserving every observation and every action taken.
Repeat the scenario with changed requirements, latency, and permissions to expose brittle plans.
Score planning, tool selection, argument validity, retries, and policy compliance at each step.
Record the starting state, the observable success condition, the allowed tools, and the required approvals.

variants.hint: Which step produces the evidence that the final message cannot supply?
variants.explanation: The contract makes success observable, and the authoritative state check is what turns a claim into a result.

variants.title: Score the whole trajectory
variants.context: An agent run is scored end to end: declare the task contract, execute in a controlled world, score the decisions and recovery along the way, verify authoritative external state, then repeat under variation. The agent's own completion sentence is never the evidence.
variants.prompt: An agent reports that a customer refund was issued, but the refund tool returned a 500 on its third call. Put the steps that settle the run in order.

items.text: Rerun the scenario with the same injected failure to check whether the behavior is reproducible.
Query the ledger to establish whether any refund exists, and whether more than one was created.
Recover the declared success condition for this scenario, which is a settled refund in the ledger.
Score the step where the agent wrote a completion message despite an unhandled tool error.
Replay the preserved observations and actions to find the failed call and what the agent did next.

variants.hint: The narrative and the ledger are two different pieces of evidence.
variants.explanation: A convincing completion message after a failed tool is exactly the failure the authoritative state check exists to catch.

variants.title: Score the whole trajectory
variants.context: An agent run is scored end to end: declare the task contract, execute in a controlled world, score the decisions and recovery along the way, verify authoritative external state, then repeat under variation. The agent's own completion sentence is never the evidence.
variants.prompt: A payment agent hits a timeout after the provider may already have committed the charge. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Score the recovery decision, separating a safe reconciliation from a blind retry.
Run the scenario with the injected timeout while recording the idempotency key sent on every attempt.
Read the provider ledger to detect a duplicate charge that no tool response reported.
Vary the timing of the delayed webhook to see whether the same recovery holds.
Confirm the scenario declared idempotency requirements and the approvals a repeated charge would need.

variants.hint: An ambiguous outcome is settled outside the agent, not inside it.
variants.explanation: Timeouts after a possible commit are a named failure surface, and only authoritative state can classify the result.

variants.title: Read the agent gates in order
variants.context: Agent release gates are read in a fixed order, and each one is independent. High task completion cannot pay for an unauthorized action, and a low cost cannot pay for a false success.
variants.prompt: A scorecard for a new agent release is on the table and the team wants to start from average task completion. Put the gates in order.

items.text: Bound the trajectory on p95 steps, latency, and cost instead of rewarding eventual success.
Inspect tool and recovery behavior, separating provider failures from malformed calls and unsafe retries.
Verify final state with a conservative completion bound rather than the agent's point estimate.
Enforce authorization separately, treating boundary violations as hard blockers.
Grant only bounded exposure with abort signals rather than unrestricted autonomy.
Measure the false-success gap to learn whether completion language can be trusted at all.

variants.hint: Start with the number that does not come from the agent itself.
variants.explanation: Verified state comes first because every later gate is read against evidence the agent could otherwise narrate.

variants.title: Read the agent gates in order
variants.context: Agent release gates are read in a fixed order, and each one is independent. High task completion cannot pay for an unauthorized action, and a low cost cannot pay for a false success.
variants.prompt: An agent verifies at 91 percent completion, reports 93 percent itself, and attempts a prohibited action in 2 percent of adversarial runs. Put the gates in order.

items.text: Note that the two point self-report gap is small, so completion language is roughly trustworthy here.
Record the p95 steps and cost for completed and failed runs separately.
Take the conservative bound on the 91 percent verified completion as the starting evidence.
Withhold exposure entirely, since a hard blocker is present.
Continue reading tool errors and recovery so the blocked release still produces a diagnosis.
Block on the 2 percent boundary violations, which the 91 percent completion is not allowed to offset.

variants.hint: Which gate is unaffected by how well the agent completes tasks?
variants.explanation: Authorization is enforced separately, so a healthy completion rate never cancels an attempted prohibited action.

variants.title: Read the agent gates in order
variants.context: Agent release gates are read in a fixed order, and each one is independent. High task completion cannot pay for an unauthorized action, and a low cost cannot pay for a false success.
variants.prompt: An agent eventually finishes almost everything, but its p95 run takes 47 steps and repeats side-effecting calls. Put the gates in order.

items.text: Hold exposure until the trajectory budget passes, rather than accepting success at any price.
Fail the trajectory budget on p95 steps and repeated side-effect risk.
Establish verified completion from authoritative state before reading anything about efficiency.
Separate provider errors from repeated identical calls and retries made without reconciliation.
Compare the self-reported and verified rates to confirm the completions are real.
Confirm no run attempted or executed a prohibited action.

variants.hint: Eventual success is still measured against a declared budget.
variants.explanation: Trajectory budgets are gated separately so an agent cannot buy completion with unbounded steps and repeated effects.

variants.title: Report the rate with its denominator
variants.context: Agent metrics are reported as counts with their denominators. Verified completion, false-success gap, and boundary violation each have a declared denominator, and changing that denominator changes what the number claims.
variants.prompt: An agent reports itself complete on 92 percent of runs, while authoritative state verification finds 71 percent complete. What is the false-success gap in percentage points?
variants.hint: The gap is a difference between two rates that were measured on the same runs.
variants.explanation: The false-success gap is self-reported completion minus verified completion. A large gap means completion language is not evidence.

mistakes.feedback: You added the two rates instead of subtracting the verified rate from the claim.
That is the verified completion rate, not the distance between claim and reality.

variants.title: Report the rate with its denominator
variants.context: Agent metrics are reported as counts with their denominators. Verified completion, false-success gap, and boundary violation each have a declared denominator, and changing that denominator changes what the number claims.
variants.prompt: A scenario set runs 50 times, but 10 runs are voided because a fixture failed to load. Authoritative state verification passes on 34 of the eligible runs. What is the verified completion rate in percent?
variants.hint: Voided runs never produced a valid outcome to verify.
variants.explanation: Verified completion is runs whose authoritative state satisfies every success condition divided by eligible runs.

mistakes.feedback: You divided by all 50 runs instead of the 40 eligible ones.
That is the failure rate among eligible runs.

variants.title: Report the rate with its denominator
variants.context: Agent metrics are reported as counts with their denominators. Verified completion, false-success gap, and boundary violation each have a declared denominator, and changing that denominator changes what the number claims.
variants.prompt: A suite has 150 runs, of which 75 are adversarial. Six runs attempt or execute a prohibited action, and 2 of those six actually execute it. What is the boundary violation rate in percent?
variants.hint: Check both which runs count in the numerator and which runs count in the denominator.
variants.explanation: The boundary violation rate counts attempted or executed prohibited actions over adversarial and representative runs together.

mistakes.feedback: You counted only the 2 executed violations; attempts count too.
You divided by the 75 adversarial runs; the denominator includes the representative runs.

variants.title: Pick the metric that answers it
variants.context: Outcome, safety, trajectory quality, and recovery are kept independent so a blended score cannot hide why a run failed. Each has its own definition and its own denominator.
variants.prompt: A scorecard lists five metrics. Match each metric to what it measures.

pairs.label: Verified completion
pairs.detail: Runs whose authoritative final state meets every success condition, over eligible runs.

pairs.label: False-success gap
pairs.detail: Self-reported completion minus externally verified completion.

pairs.label: Boundary violation
pairs.detail: Runs with an attempted or executed prohibited action, over adversarial and representative runs.

pairs.label: Tool error and recovery
pairs.detail: Failed calls by error type, and the share recovered without duplicate or unsafe effects.

pairs.label: Trajectory budget
pairs.detail: The p50 and p95 steps, latency, and cost, reported for completed and failed runs separately.

variants.hint: Two of these are about what the agent did, and two are about what actually happened outside it.
variants.explanation: Each metric keeps its own denominator so that outcome, safety, efficiency, and recovery cannot be traded against one another.

variants.title: Pick the metric that answers it
variants.context: Outcome, safety, trajectory quality, and recovery are kept independent so a blended score cannot hide why a run failed. Each has its own definition and its own denominator.
variants.prompt: Five observations come out of one evaluation batch. Match each observation to the metric that exposes it.

pairs.label: Verified completion
pairs.detail: The ledger shows only 68 of 100 eligible tasks in the requested end state.

pairs.label: False-success gap
pairs.detail: The agent declares success 19 points more often than the environment confirms it.

pairs.label: Boundary violation
pairs.detail: Four adversarial runs try to read a record belonging to another tenant.

pairs.label: Tool error and recovery
pairs.detail: Half the timeouts are followed by a retry with no reconciliation step.

pairs.label: Trajectory budget
pairs.detail: Failed runs burn a median of 38 steps before giving up.

variants.hint: Ask which number each observation would move if it were reported honestly.
variants.explanation: Reporting each observation under its own metric is what stops one blended score from hiding the reason for the failure.

variants.title: Pick the metric that answers it
variants.context: Outcome, safety, trajectory quality, and recovery are kept independent so a blended score cannot hide why a run failed. Each has its own definition and its own denominator.
variants.prompt: A release reviewer asks five questions. Match each question to the metric that answers it.

pairs.label: Verified completion
pairs.detail: Did the external system actually reach the state the user asked for?

pairs.label: False-success gap
pairs.detail: Can we trust the agent's own completion language as a signal?

pairs.label: Boundary violation
pairs.detail: Did any run cross a permission or approval boundary?

pairs.label: Tool error and recovery
pairs.detail: When a call failed, did the agent recover without duplicating an effect?

pairs.label: Trajectory budget
pairs.detail: How expensive is the slow tail of runs, whether or not they finished?

variants.hint: One of these questions is answered by comparing two numbers rather than reading one.
variants.explanation: A useful scorecard maps each release question to one metric with a stated denominator.

variants.title: Refuse the unsafe shortcut
variants.context: Efficiency is only meaningful once a run is verified and authorized. A run that crosses a permission boundary, leaves an unreconciled side effect, or falsely claims completion has no efficiency score to compare.
variants.prompt: Agent A finishes a scenario in two tool calls but skips a required approval. Agent B finishes the same scenario in five calls with every approval in place.
options: Withhold an efficiency score for agent A, because the run crossed an approval boundary.
Prefer agent A, since it reached the same end state with fewer tool calls.
Report both efficiency scores and let the reviewer weigh calls against approvals.
optionFeedback: The efficiency score is blocked entirely when a run violates permissions or bypasses an approval.
Fewer calls is not efficiency when one of the skipped steps was a required approval.
Presenting the unauthorized run as comparable invites a trade that the gate forbids.
variants.hint: Ask whether these two runs are comparable at all.
variants.explanation: An agent making one unauthorized call is not more efficient than an agent making three safe calls.

variants.title: Refuse the unsafe shortcut
variants.context: Efficiency is only meaningful once a run is verified and authorized. A run that crosses a permission boundary, leaves an unreconciled side effect, or falsely claims completion has no efficiency score to compare.
variants.prompt: An evaluator has the agent's final message, the tool responses, and a judge rating of the message, but no read access to the billing system.
options: Score the run complete, since the refund tool returned a success response.
Score the run complete, since the judge rated the completion message as coherent.
Score the run unverified, because no authoritative state read was available.
optionFeedback: A success response is a tool claim, and the failure mode being tested is exactly a claim without an effect.
A coherent message measures writing quality, not whether the money moved.
Without an authoritative read the run has no verified outcome, so it cannot count as complete.
variants.hint: Which of these three sources sits outside the agent and its tools?
variants.explanation: Never accept a success claim without joining it to authoritative external state.

variants.title: Refuse the unsafe shortcut
variants.context: Efficiency is only meaningful once a run is verified and authorized. A run that crosses a permission boundary, leaves an unreconciled side effect, or falsely claims completion has no efficiency score to compare.
variants.prompt: One scenario is a straight-line lookup and another requires recovering from two injected tool failures. Both agents are ranked on total tool calls.
options: Rank on calls divided by steps so that longer runs are normalized automatically.
Rank within scenario families so recovery work is compared against recovery work.
Rank on total tool calls, since the same budget should apply to every scenario.
optionFeedback: Dividing calls by steps rescales the number without making the two scenarios comparable.
Comparing inside a scenario family keeps difficulty constant while efficiency varies.
A shared budget punishes the agent that was handed the harder scenario.
variants.hint: What else changed between the two scenarios besides the agent?
variants.explanation: Tool-call count is meaningful only when conditioned on task difficulty and a verified outcome.
